summary: Outlines a possible but not recommended method to reduce the effect of collisions in the DNS namespace by giving end users a way to disambiguate the conflict.

plainLanguage.summary: Two names may point to different things. This describes a way, which the author does not suggest, to let a user choose which one they meant.

subtitle: Outlines a discouraged approach to resolving DNS name collisions.

tldr.problem: DNS namespace collisions occur when a name could refer to either an internal resource or a newly-delegated TLD; users cannot disambiguate.
tldr.mechanism: One approach is to show the user multiple options and let them choose, either through a resolver shim, a browser dialog, or an interstitial page.
tldr.outcome: The RFC explicitly recommends against this approach due to security and usability problems: humans may not know the correct answer, it introduces latency, and it creates phishing risks.

today: RFC 7304 documents an approach explicitly not recommended. It shows the pitfalls of user-facing disambiguation and explains why the namespace collision problem requires other solutions.

sections.title: The Collision Problem
sections.content: DNS collisions happen when the same domain name refers to different things in different places. A common case: a company uses 'www.foo.example.com' internally for corporate servers, but then 'foo' is delegated as a new top-level domain. When an employee types 'www.foo', does it mean the internal machine or the public website on the 'foo' TLD? The browser or resolver cannot know without asking.
sections.plainLanguage: When you type a short name, computers need to guess whether you mean something at your office or something public on the internet. Sometimes they guess wrong.

sections.title: The User-Choice Approach
sections.content:
One mitigation is to look up the name in multiple places and, if a collision is detected, present the options to the user and let them choose. This could be done at the resolver level (a library wrapper), in the browser, or through a proxy that shows an interstitial page asking which site you meant.

The system could also cache the user's choice or let them set preferences for which version they prefer.
sections.plainLanguage: When there is a collision, show the user a page that says: 'Did you mean the internal server or the public website?' and let them pick.

sections.title: Why This Approach Fails
sections.content: The RFC identifies serious problems with this approach. First, not all systems have a human available: mail servers, background services, and unattended machines cannot answer a question. Second, even when a human is present, they may not know the correct answer, especially in phishing attacks where a malicious site mimics a legitimate one. Third, the extra latency and user interaction for every collision is time-consuming, especially if the user must disambiguate many related names (www.intranet, images.intranet, etc.). Finally, caching creates problems: a user's choice that is correct in the office is wrong when they are at home.
sections.plainLanguage: Computers may not have anyone to ask. Users might pick the wrong one. It is slow. And if the office setting changes, the cached choice stops working.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.content: RFC 7304 documents an approach that has many serious problems and is explicitly not recommended. The namespace collision problem is real, but this mitigation does not solve it. Better solutions, such as avoiding the use of ambiguous short names and careful corporate naming practices, are far preferable to burdening every user with disambiguation choices.
sections.plainLanguage: Asking users to pick is a bad solution. It is better to avoid the problem by using clear, unambiguous names.
